skills.name: The octet rule: noble gas configuration

note.text:
Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar) are very unreactive because their outer shell is full: 2 for helium, 8 for the others (an octet).
Octet rule: atoms react by losing, gaining or sharing electrons so that they end up with a full outer shell like the nearest noble gas.
• Metals with 1, 2 or 3 outer electrons lose them: Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8), like neon.
• Non-metals with 5, 6 or 7 outer electrons gain 3, 2 or 1: O (2,6) → O²⁻ (2,8), like neon.
• Non-metals can also share electrons to complete their octets (covalent bonds).

sections.heading: Why noble gases are special
sections.text:
Helium, neon and argon hardly react at all. Their outer shells are full: {2} electrons for helium, {8} for neon and argon.
A full outer shell is a very stable arrangement. Eight outer electrons is called an octet.

sections.heading: The octet rule
sections.text:
Other atoms react in ways that give them a full outer shell, like the nearest noble gas.
• Metals have {1}, {2} or {3} outer electrons. It is easiest to lose them: sodium ({2}, {8}, {1}) becomes Na⁺ ({2}, {8}).
• Non-metals have {5}, {6} or {7}. It is easiest to gain the few that are missing: chlorine ({2}, {8}, {7}) becomes Cl⁻ ({2}, {8}, {8}).
• Two non-metals can also share electrons so that both complete their octets.

sections.heading: Predicting the charge
sections.text:
Losing electrons gives a positive ion; gaining gives a negative ion:
• group I → +{1}; group II → +{2}; group III → +{3};
• group V → −{3}; group VI → −{2}; group VII → −{1}.
So aluminium forms Al³⁺ and oxygen forms O²⁻.

key_words.meaning: eight electrons in the outer shell
a full outer shell like He, Ne or Ar

mistake.wrong: Chlorine loses {7} electrons to empty its outer shell
mistake.right: Chlorine gains {1} electron to complete its octet
mistake.why: Gaining one electron is far easier than losing seven.

worked_example.problem: Sulphur has atomic number {z}. How does it reach a noble gas configuration, and what ion forms?
steps: Gaining {8 - outerElectrons(z)} is easier than losing {outerElectrons(z)}.
It gains {8 - outerElectrons(z)} electrons: {shells(z + 8 - outerElectrons(z))}, like argon. The ion is S²⁻.
worked_example.answer: It gains {8 - outerElectrons(z)} electrons to form S²⁻

cards.idea: A full outer shell (an octet, or {2} for helium) is stable.
example: Neon {2}, {8} and argon {2}, {8}, {8} do not react.

cards.idea: Metals lose their {1}, {2} or {3} outer electrons.

check.prompt: How many electrons does {nameOf(X)} (atomic number {z}) gain to reach a noble gas configuration?

misconceptions.explain: Non-metals with {outerElectrons(z)} outer electrons gain electrons rather than losing so many.

solution: It needs {8} − {outerElectrons(z)} = {answer} more to complete the octet.

pick.q: Why are the noble gases unreactive?
w: They are too heavy to react
e: They have electrons in full shells.
pick.y: A full outer shell is a stable arrangement.

pick.q: What does the octet rule say?
pick.r: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to get eight in the outer shell
e: Most atoms do not have eight outer electrons to start with.
They gain or lose only what they need.
pick.y: Eight outer electrons, like a noble gas, is stable.

pick.q: Which ion has the same electron arrangement as neon (2, 8)?

questions.prompt: How many electrons does {nameOf(X)} (atomic number {z}) lose to reach a noble gas configuration?

misconceptions.explain: Metals lose their few outer electrons rather than gaining many.

solution: It loses all {answer} to leave a full shell.

questions.prompt: How many electrons does {nameOf(X)} (atomic number {z}) gain to reach a noble gas configuration?

misconceptions.explain: Non-metals with {outerElectrons(z)} outer electrons gain electrons rather than losing so many.

solution: It needs {8} − {outerElectrons(z)} = {answer} more to complete the octet.

questions.prompt: What is the charge of the ion formed by {nameOf(X)} (atomic number {z})? Give a signed number, e.g. −1.

misconceptions.explain: Losing electrons gives a positive ion; gaining gives a negative ion.

solution: {outerElectrons(z) <= 3 ? 'It loses ' + outerElectrons(z) + ' electron(s), so the ion is positive.' : 'It gains ' + (8 - outerElectrons(z)) + ' electron(s), so the ion is negative.'} Charge {answer}.
